item.title: Mainland to expand market access for Taiwan farm and fishery products
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29
Mainland to expand market access for Taiwan farm and fishery products BEIJING, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese mainland will continue implementing the 10 measures issued in April to promote cross-Strait exchanges and cooperation, including helping Taiwan's farmers and fishermen expand sales on the mainland, a spokesperson said on Wednesday. Chen Binhua, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular press conference that the measures, announced on April 12, had helped widen distribution channels for Taiwan's pomelos, custard apples and other agricultural products. The efforts are based on adhering to the 1992 Consensus and opposing "Taiwan independence," which aims to improve the livelihoods of Taiwan people, Chen said. In mid-October, about 350 tonnes of Taiwan's signature seafood had arrived in Xiamen, east China's Fujian Province, Chen said. Shortly after, a Taiwan fishery products exhibition and sales center opened, alongside a cross-Strait seafood market and a fishery culture exhibition. The mainland has long been an important export market for Taiwan's seafood, which is popular with mainland consumers given similar dietary habits on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, he said. Future efforts will continue to see Taiwan's agricultural, fishery and other quality products reach consumers on the mainland. Chen said the mainland had also responded to concerns among Taiwan's fishing communities by organizing business-matching and signing events, streamlining customs procedures and supporting participation in trade fairs. In the first three quarters of this year, mainland imports of agricultural products from Taiwan rose 18.5 percent year on year, while fishery product imports increased 35.5 percent, he said. From April to September, Fujian imported 19,100 tonnes of fishery products from Taiwan, with a total value of 585 million yuan (about 87 million U.S. dollars), up 35.9 percent year on year. The mainland will continue to share development opportunities with Taiwan compatriots and assist in addressing practical difficulties, Chen said. The goal is to enable people on both sides of the Strait to gain greater benefits from cross-Strait economic and trade cooperation and integrated development and enjoy better lives, he added.

item.title: Mainland condemns DPP's use of public funds for US observers at Taiwan drills
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29
Mainland condemns DPP's use of public funds for US observers at Taiwan drills A Chinese mainland spokesman on Wednesday condemned the Democratic Progressive Party authorities for spending public funds to invite US personnel to observe Taiwan's military drills, emphasizing that the Taiwan question does not tolerate external interference. At a regular news conference, Chen Binhua, spokesman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, accused the DPP authorities of wasting the hard-earned money of Taiwan residents in a futile attempt to pursue "Taiwan independence" through force and external support. Taiwan's "defense" department recently acknowledged earmarking approximately NT$82.44 million ($2.54 million) for this year and next to invite US personnel, including a retired US general, to observe the so-called Han Kuang exercises, the island's largest annual military drills. "The Taiwan question is purely an internal affair of China, and no external interference will be tolerated," Chen stated. He added that the DPP authorities' pursuit of "Taiwan independence" is misguided and doomed to fail. The DPP authorities' decision also drew criticism on the island, with public opinion accusing them of "pleading poverty to the people while being generous to outsiders".

item.title: Mainland calls on Taiwan entertainers to embrace Chinese identity
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29
Mainland calls on Taiwan entertainers to embrace Chinese identity A Chinese mainland spokesman on Wednesday called on entertainers in Taiwan to take pride in their Chinese identity and contribute to closer ties and greater exchanges between people across the Taiwan Strait. Chen Binhua, spokesman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular news conference that safeguarding national sovereignty and territorial integrity is a common obligation of all Chinese people, including Taiwan compatriots. His remarks came in response to Taiwan entertainer Tsai Kang-yong, also known as Kevin Tsai, who recently said he had never supported "Taiwan independence" after appearing at a campaign event for Shen Pao-yang, the Democratic Progressive Party candidate for the Taipei mayoral election. Shen was listed by the mainland as a diehard "Taiwan independence" separatist in 2024. Tsai's appearance at Shen's campaign event prompted several mainland companies to end their cooperation with him. As a famous television host, Tsai has been active on both sides of the Taiwan Strait in recent years. On Sunday evening, Tsai posted on mainland social media that he had always supported friendly cross-Strait exchanges and had never supported "Taiwan independence". He said he had visited events attended by various interviewees to gather information and make observations, and apologized for any confusion caused by his actions. "We always respect and protect the legitimate freedom of speech and expression of Taiwan compatriots," the spokesman said. "However, there is no room for ambiguity on matters of fundamental importance concerning national sovereignty, security and development interests." Chen also called on Taiwan entertainers to take pride in being Chinese and contribute more to strengthening the bonds between people across the Taiwan Strait and promoting cross-Strait exchanges and cooperation.

item.title: Taiwan to prosper from peaceful reunification
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-28
Taiwan to prosper from peaceful reunification Editor's note:The Taiwan question is a key focus for China and the international community. China Daily is publishing a series of reports to track hot Taiwan-related topics and address disinformation from the Democratic Progressive Party administration. Young people from both sides of the Taiwan Strait tour Fuzhou Panda World in Fuzhou, Fujian province, on Jan 27. XINHUA Following a peaceful cross-Strait reunification and backed by a strong motherland, Taiwan will no longer need massive "defense" expenditures, meaning its fiscal revenue can be fully dedicated to improving public welfare and ensuring residents live in peace and prosperity, experts said. At the Commemoration Day of Taiwan's Restoration on Oct 25 last year, the Chinese mainland proposed a landmark vision outlining how Taiwan will be better across seven major aspects after peaceful reunification, sparking a profound and rational discussion across the Strait over how Taiwan compatriots can achieve genuine security and an upgraded standard of living. This long-term vision stands in sharp contrast to the current realities under the island's Democratic Progressive Party authorities, who have sparked heavy criticism for driving next year's planned defense budget to a record 1.3 trillion New Taiwan dollars ($39.9 billion) while showing extreme reluctance to fund a modest NT$40 billion health insurance subsidy for senior residents. Chiu Chih-shien, secretary-general of the Taiwan Restoration Commemoration Association, said that the Lai Ching-te authorities have neglected public welfare, instead squandering massive funds on self-serving projects including military purchases. Chiu noted that the current authorities have leaned completely toward the United States, creating an unequal relationship where Washington makes endless demands. "Taiwan is forced to swallow a bitter pill in silence, leaving many residents feeling resentful," he said, adding that such a submissive stance neither enhances their dignity nor brings a better life. Zhu Guilan, an assistant professor at Tsinghua University's Institute for Taiwan Studies, said that the DPP authorities have deliberately fostered a sense of insecurity among the Taiwan public to justify their so-called defense buildup. She pointed out that this approach has trapped the island in a vicious cycle where increased military spending only breeds greater anxiety. Zhu said that weapons purchased from the US are often outdated, delayed in delivery and useless in actual combat. Reports showed that the total backlog of delayed US arms deliveries to Taiwan has ballooned to a record $29.72 billion, leaving the island trapped in chronic delivery delays. Furthermore, Zhu noted that high-profile maneuvers like this year's so-called Han Kuang exercises failed to safeguard Taiwan, serving only to brainwash residents with a confrontational mindset, which is never the root of real security. "The only way to truly eliminate this anxiety is peaceful reunification with the mainland," she said, adding that if these massive military expenditures were instead redirected toward infrastructure and education, it would bring immense benefits to Taiwan's next generation. Lai Yueh-tchien, a Taiwan political commentator, said that Taiwan's pressing power shortages for artificial intelligence development, semiconductor manufacturing and daily life could be easily resolved if the island accepted abundant clean energy supplied by the Chinese mainland. "There is absolutely no technical difficulty in transmitting this continuous flow of clean energy, and the mainland is highly willing to do so," Lai said, questioning why the authorities refuse an option that would eliminate Taiwan's electricity crisis and the need for controversial nuclear plants. In stark contrast to the heavy financial burdens imposed by the Lai authorities, a growing number of Taiwan compatriots are finding a prosperous, convenient and satisfying life on the Chinese mainland.

item.title: One-China principle emphasized
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-26
One-China principle emphasized Cross-Strait representatives gathered on Sunday to mark the 81st anniversary of Taiwan's restoration to the motherland, stressing that both sides belong to one China and expressing firm opposition to "Taiwan independence" separatism and external interference. A symposium in Fu-zhou, Fujian province, brought together around 200 attendees, including descendants of revolutionary martyrs who sacrificed their lives in Taiwan and Taiwan compatriots who resisted Japanese aggression, cross-Strait youth, experts, scholars and representatives from the Hong Kong and Macao special administrative regions and overseas. The event came one year after a decision by the national legislature to designate Oct 25 as the Commemoration Day of Taiwan's Restoration, the day in 1945 when Taiwan was officially returned to China after half a century of Japanese colonial occupation. Song Tao, head of the Taiwan Work Office of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said that the establishment of the commemorative day demonstrated the country's firm confidence in defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity, and solidified the international community's adherence to the one-China principle. Song emphasized that compatriots on both sides of the Taiwan Strait must jointly carry forward the great spirit of the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45), while firmly opposing "Taiwan independence" separatism and external interference. It is essential to promote Chinese culture to strengthen national pride and boost the confidence of the Chinese people, he said, adding that the Chinese mainland will firmly support the patriotic reunification forces within the island and steadfastly advance national reunification. Hung Hsiu-chu, former chairwoman of the Chinese Kuomintang party, recalled the crimes committed by the Japanese aggressors against Chinese people and warned that people must remain strictly vigilant against Japan's attempts to revive militarism. Hung criticized Taiwan's current Democratic Progressive Party authorities for attempting to erase the history of the war against Japanese invasion and Taiwan's restoration from the school curriculum, which she said left younger generations unaware of their roots and created a confused identity that remained a fundamental cause of Taiwan's internal rift and cross-Strait tensions. Ou Kuei-chih, a retired Chinese literature teacher from Taipei First Girls' High School, said that only by learning history can young people discover their roots, understand the past suffering of the nation, and find answers on how to avoid the danger of war caused by cross-Strait division. Encouraging Taiwan youths to visit the mainland for more exchanges, she said students must break through the bias of the island's media to search for the truth, explore why textbooks differ, and make their own rational judgments. Chiu Chih-shien, secretary-general of the Taiwan Restoration Commemoration Association, said that Taiwan's restoration was a core achievement of the war against Japanese aggression, noting that this historic day was once widely celebrated through various public activities before the DPP's deliberate erasure led to its gradual fading from public memory over the past decades. Chiu said that the legislation last year had prompted many Taiwan compatriots to reflect on why local textbooks and media in Taiwan remained silent while the mainland highly valued the anniversary, inspiring people to recognize its true historical value. He added that civic groups on the island should work together to hold more public activities so that people can learn the real history and understand how restoration benefits them.

item.title: Xinhua Commentary: Marking Taiwan Recovery Day with shared resolve to advance China's reunification
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-25
Xinhua Commentary: Marking Taiwan Recovery Day with shared resolve to advance China's reunification Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-10-25
BEIJING, Oct. 24 (Xinhua) -- As China prepares to mark the 81st anniversary of its recovery of Taiwan and observe the Taiwan Recovery Day on Oct. 25, the occasion offers an opportunity to revisit a glorious chapter of history, in which people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait jointly resisted foreign aggression, and to draw strength from the past to advance reunification. China's recovery of Taiwan in 1945 was a hard-won victory in the Chinese people's resistance against Japanese aggression during World War II, and a defining moment in the nation's struggle to safeguard its sovereignty and territorial integrity. Starting in 1840, China endured a period of immense suffering amid foreign aggression and the decay of feudal rule. Japan's aggression marked some of the darkest chapters in modern Chinese history. Following its war against China in 1894, Japan seized Taiwan and the Penghu Islands in 1895, subjecting Taiwan to five decades of colonial rule. Faced with both internal turmoil and foreign invasion, the Chinese people valiantly fought against the invaders, ultimately defeating Japanese aggression to safeguard the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity. On Oct. 25, 1945, after China's victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the broader World Anti-Fascist War, Taiwan was recovered. This historic day, forever etched in the history of the Chinese nation, deserves to be remembered by people on both sides of the Strait. Throughout the struggles against foreign aggression and for national liberation, Taiwan shared the fate of its motherland China. Patriots in Taiwan resisted Japanese colonial rule through political, military and cultural struggles, with more than 650,000 giving their lives during the five decades of Japanese occupation. Driven by the conviction that "to save Taiwan, one must first save the motherland," over 50,000 people in Taiwan went across the Strait to join the fight against Japanese aggression, risking their lives to defend the dignity and honor of the Chinese nation. Historical archives and photographs capture the island's jubilant celebrations when China recovered Taiwan in 1945. Families decorated their homes with lanterns, brought out ancestral tablets, and burned incense to share the good news with their forebears. Residents poured spontaneously into streets to cheer, while the sound of firecrackers rang out into the night. These memories, forged through bloodshed and sacrifice, testify to the deep-rooted bonds between people in Taiwan and their fellow Chinese on the mainland, as well as the shared destiny of people on both sides of the Strait. China's recovery of Taiwan was an important outcome of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, and provides compelling evidence that the Chinese government resumed the exercise of sovereignty over Taiwan. The Cairo Declaration, issued in 1943, stipulates that all territories Japan had stolen from China, including Taiwan and the Penghu Islands, shall be restored to China. The Potsdam Proclamation of 1945 reiterates that "the terms of the Cairo Declaration shall be carried out." In September 1945, Japan signed the instrument of surrender, pledging to fulfill the obligations set out in the Potsdam Proclamation. On Oct. 25 that year, the Chinese government announced that it was resuming its exercise of sovereignty over Taiwan. A ceremony to accept Japan's surrender in Taiwan Province of the China war theater of the Allied powers was held in Taipei. From that point forward, China had recovered Taiwan de jure and de facto through a host of documents with international legal effect. Taiwan's status as an inalienable part of the Chinese territory was thereby reaffirmed, and the question of Taiwan's status was resolved. However, an unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left the two sides of the Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. The fact that the two sides of the Taiwan Strait have yet to be fully reunified is a scar left by history on the Chinese nation, but the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed. Driven by their political interests and secessionist agenda, Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and other secessionist forces have repeatedly claimed that Taiwan's status remains undetermined, distorted historical accounts in textbooks, pursued educational policies that remove Chinese cultural elements, and propagated a separatist narrative in an attempt to sever historical ties across the Strait and mislead younger generations in Taiwan. Since Lai Ching-te took office in 2024, the DPP authorities have conspicuously avoided mentioning China's victory in the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression and China's recovery of Taiwan. The DPP authorities have also repeatedly downplayed or whitewashed Japan's colonial rule over Taiwan. Such actions betray the fundamental interests of the Chinese nation. Achieving national reunification is a responsibility shared by all Chinese people, including people in Taiwan. The establishment of the Taiwan Recovery Day enables people on both sides of the Strait to commemorate this historic moment together. The Taiwan question originated in a weak and ravaged China, and will be resolved as China achieves national rejuvenation. Commemorating Taiwan's recovery today is an opportunity to draw strength and resolve from the sacrifices of the war and the recovery of lost territory, while reaffirming the determination and confidence to advance national reunification. item.title: Mainland to strengthen CPC-KMT platform for protecting Taiwan people's rights
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22
Mainland to strengthen CPC-KMT platform for protecting Taiwan people's rights Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-10-22
BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese mainland will work to improve the operation and effectiveness of a cross-Strait platform established by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT), a spokesperson said Wednesday. The platform has maintained effective operations over the years through regular meetings, case referrals and other forms of cooperation, making itself an important channel for people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait to lodge complaints, seek advice and assistance, and protect their legitimate rights and interests, Zhang Han, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular news briefing. Since the beginning of this year, the Taiwan Work Office of the CPC Central Committee and the KMT have held multiple consultations to improve the platform's operations and effectiveness, and they have reached a consensus on further cooperation, she said. The two sides will maintain regular communication and provide timely feedback, and the platform will offer Taiwan residents professional legal services, Zhang said. They will also work to enhance assistance for Taiwan residents facing temporary difficulties, help people search for missing relatives and provide humanitarian care, she added. The two sides of the Strait established an investment dispute settlement mechanism in 2012 under a cross-Strait investment protection agreement reached on a common political foundation of the 1992 Consensus. However, the mechanism was suspended in May 2016 because Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities refused to recognize the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, Zhang said. The mainland is willing to engage in dialogue on resuming the mechanism's operations, provided that the DPP authorities recognize the 1992 Consensus, Zhang said. The Taiwan question stems from a civil war fought between the forces led by the CPC and the KMT about eight decades ago. In 1949, the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, while the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC. The unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left the two sides of the Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed. Related Stories

item.title: Mainland denounces Taiwan authorities for hindering cross-Strait exchanges
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21
Mainland denounces Taiwan authorities for hindering cross-Strait exchanges Source: XinhuaUpdated: 2026-10-21
BEIJING, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday criticized the Taiwan authorities for barring relevant people on the island from attending the commemorative event held on the mainland marking the 160th anniversary of the birth of Sun Yat-sen. Sun, a founding figure of the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) and a revered revolutionary leader who played a pivotal role in overthrowing imperial rule in China, died in 1925 in Beijing. His remains rest at the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province. Zhang Han, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, noted that the grand commemoration of Sun's legacy is intended to inherit and carry forward his noble spirit of upholding national unity and striving for national rejuvenation. She stressed that the move by Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party authorities to obstruct cross-Strait exchanges and suppress Taiwan compatriots fully exposes their vicious intentions of betraying the nation and history, seeking to split the country, and stoking confrontation across the Taiwan Strait. The Taiwan question stems from China's civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the KMT about eight decades ago. In 1949, the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC. The unresolved civil war, combined with foreign interference, has kept the two sides of the Taiwan Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed. Related Stories

item.title: Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges
item.description:
Published: 2026-02-11
Taiwan's DPP authorities slammed for obstructing cross-Strait exchanges BEIJING, Feb. 11 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson has condemned Taiwan's Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities for imposing restrictions and obstacles on cross-Strait exchanges in pursuit of their "Taiwan independence" agenda and selfish gains. The DPP authorities, led by Lai Ching-te, are the biggest obstacle to cross-Strait interactions and their acts have drawn strong criticism from various sectors in Taiwan, Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said at a regular press briefing on Wednesday. Zhu expressed the hope that Taiwan compatriots will firmly oppose the retrogressive actions of the DPP authorities and promote exchanges and cooperation across the Taiwan Strait in various fields. She noted that cross-Strait flight routes have been disrupted due to interference from the DPP authorities, with previously operated destinations yet to resume normal operations. In 2025, the average passenger load factor on cross-Strait routes reached 80 percent, reflecting the strong need for direct flights between the two sides of the Strait, Zhu said. "We hope that the Taiwan side will heed public opinion and lift unreasonable restrictions on cross-Strait air transport as soon as possible," she added.
